The New York Times has reported that the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) may have waterboarded more people than it previously admitted.

Durham’s probe ended without any criminal charges. But The New York Times obtained partially redacted documents from his investigation, including a summary of a 2012 interview with an interpreter who described a previously unconfirmed act of waterboarding.
The account sheds new light on one of the most infamous methods of torture utilised by the intelligence agency after the attacks on September 11, 2001.
Waterboarding involves restraining a person and pouring water on their face through a cloth, to mimic the experience of drowning.
The CIA called the practice an “enhanced interrogation technique”. As part of the US’s so-called “war on terror”, the agency sent suspects to overseas prisons, known as black sites, where they would be tortured in secret, including through waterboarding.
While the practice was shielded from scrutiny for years, a 2009 executive order eventually barred continued waterboarding. Congress has likewise passed restrictions.

item.title: [CBS News World] Germany arrests 2 Iraqis allegedly tied to Iran-linked terror group
item.description:
Berlin — German authorities on Thursday arrested two Iraqi men on suspicion of terrorism. The suspects are alleged to be members of an Iran-linked terrorist organization that is said to have targeted U.S., Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe.
The men, who were arrested in Cologne and Heidelberg by the Federal Criminal Police Office, are Iraqi nationals Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., according to the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office.
The investigation centers on alleged links to Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, a shadowy group that emerged to claim a series of sabotage, arson and violent attacks targeting Jewish institutions in Europe not long after the start of the U.S. war with Iran. The U.S. government has labeled HAYI a front for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah in Iraq. Britain has designated HAYI as a terrorist organization.
According to investigators, Mostafa Al-R. is alleged to have maintained contact with Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is currently facing criminal charges in the United States. Al-Saadi is considered a central figure within the alleged terrorist network.
As early as late 2025, Al-Saadi, Mostafa Al-R. and other individuals allegedly founded an independent group whose goal was to carry out terrorist attacks in Germany and other European countries, according to prosecutors. Ameer J. is also a member of this group, they said.
The group planned to target synagogues in Cologne and another European city, prosecutors alleged, saying unknown perpetrators traveled to the locations in March 2026 on behalf of the organization. The plans were not implemented for unknown reasons.
HAYI is also linked to attacks on Jewish institutions in the United Kingdom, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution said.
The suspects are accused of membership in a domestic terrorist organization under Section 129a of Germany's Criminal Code. ...

item.description:
Spain's former central bank head chosen as next European Central Bank president
Eurozone leaders have chosen a new president of the European Central BankByDAVID MCHUGH Associated Press and SAM MCNEIL Associated PressNovember 26, 2026, 10:46 AM
BRUSSELS -- European leaders have chosen the former head of Spain’s central bank, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank as the key EU institution confronts inflation driven by the war in Iran and worries about high government debt and borrowing costs in Europe.
Leaders from the 21 European member countries that use the euro also filled two other top posts at the ECB, which decides borrowing costs for the 359 million people in the eurozone.
European Council President António Costa said on X that the body agreed on the three appointments at a summit in Brussels.
De Cos’ nomination still must pass review by the European Parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but those steps are formalities.
The appointment puts an experienced central banker with a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus in charge at a time when several European governments are struggling with heavy debt loads and rising borrowing costs. De Cos, 55, served on the ECB rate-setting council from 2018 to 2024 through his post as head of the Spanish central bank.
A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.
De Cos won out over another main contender for the post, former Netherlands central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favors higher rates to ward off inflation.

item.description:
Constanța, Romania – Out on the Black Sea, the Romanian Navy is always on the lookout for the deadly debris of a war it isn't fighting.
It's a front of the Russia-Ukraine war that most people rarely see. It runs right up to NATO's doorstep and sometimes crosses into its waters — threatening to pull the alliance, and therefore the United States, into the war.
Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships are surging in the Black Sea, NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell told CBS News.
"In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea. This year alone, we're talking four to five hundred," he said.
American NATO spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News in November 2026 that the Black Sea may be "more important" than the Strait of Hormuz.
CBS News
The roughly tenfold increase threatens a major artery of global grain and fuel shipments and has made the waterway deadlier than the Strait of Hormuz, a flashpoint in the U.S.-Iran war, with both sides trying to enforce blockades on the chokepoint to exert economic pressure on the other.
Twenty-five sailors have been killed in the strait this year, according to the International Maritime Organization, while at least 40 have been killed in the Black Sea in the same period, according to the International Transport Workers' Federation.
"I would say the Black Sea is just as important, and then depending on who you talk to, some might argue could perhaps even be more important … in terms of global trade," said O'Donnell.
Any imbalance in the flow of fuel and food "can have global implications that can impact America just as much as it can any of the nations here," he said.

EU leaders seek to agree on a budget deal and a new loan for Ukraine
European Union leaders are struggling to agree on a long-term budget and more money for Ukraine in the shape of a new $49 billion loanByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 11:35 AM
Share
BRUSSELS -- European Union leaders struggled on Thursday to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree a new $49 billion loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.
At a summit in Brussels, some leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget. Most want extra funds for important new priorities, and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.
“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time there is a series of tasks we must fulfill reliably.”
“The priorities must be a flourishing economy, the internal market must be able to develop its full potential, and we need better defense,” he told reporters.
The new joint spending package is a statement of the EU’s ambitions in the world. It’s small compared to national budgets and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies.
The 2028-2034 plan could amount to between 1% and 1.2% of gross national income, but it appears increasingly likely that the leaders might well miss an end-of-year goal to agree on it.
Germany is one of an important group of so-called net contributors that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, along with Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden, among others.
“The budget needs to be modernized and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said as he arrived for the summit. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”

item.description:
UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their childrenByDANICA KIRKA Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 7:06 AM
Share
LONDON -- Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children.
Andy Burnham made the announcement Tuesday night on the BBC’s “Newsnight” program, saying the panel’s chairman would be “relentless in his pursuit of the facts.” An estimated 22,000 British military personnel witnessed Cold War-era nuclear weapons tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans from 1952 to 1967.
“Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish,” Burnham said in a statement.
Veterans claim Britain’s Ministry of Defense intentionally hid data from blood and urine samples that would demonstrate how they were unwittingly used as test subjects to investigate the impact of nuclear explosions on humans.
Former Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood said in September that he had “inadvertently misled” Parliament in 2018 when he told lawmakers the ministry had been unable to locate any information about such blood testing. He later learned that blood samples were taken throughout the military, although veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses related to radiation exposure were unable to access them.
“This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed,” Ellwood wrote in the Guardian.
Britain has no dedicated compensation program for nuclear veterans, unlike the United States. France, which conducted tes...

item.title: [BBC World] German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
item.description:

Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica Parker, Berlin correspondent and Tom Beal, BBC News InvestigationsPublished26 November 2026, 05:00 GMT
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.
The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffsByMichael Race, Jonathan Josephs and Osmond Chia, Business reportersPublished25 November 2026Updated 26 November 2026 04:10 GMT
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blazeByGrace Tsoi, BBC World Service, Phoebe Kong, BBC Chinese , Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette TanPublished25 November 2026
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.
It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.
Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
